title: Κύων καὶ κόχλος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 181. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὠά τις κύων καταπίνειν εἰθισμένος, ἰδών τινα κόχλον, χάνας τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ, μεγίστῃ συνολκῇ καταπέπωκε τοῦτον, οἰηθεὶς ᾠὸν εἶναι.
sentences.tr: Ōa tis kyōn katapinein eithismenos, idōn tina kochlon, chanas to stoma autou, megistēi synolkēi katapepōke touton, oiētheis ōion einai.
sentences.l: A certain dog, accustomed to gulping down eggs, having seen a shellfish, having gaped his mouth wide, with a very great draught has swallowed it down, thinking it to be an egg.
sentences.i: A dog in the habit of gulping eggs down saw a shellfish, opened his mouth wide, and with one enormous draught swallowed it whole, supposing it to be an egg.
sentences.n: The plural at the head is printed Ὠά, without the iota subscript that the lower-case ᾠόν carries later in the same fable; a capital omega regularly goes without it, so the difference is one of typesetting and not of word. εἰθισμένος is the perfect passive of ἐθίζω, 'having been made accustomed', with the infinitive of what one is used to doing. χάσκω is to gape. συνολκή is a drawing-in, the pull of a single swallow. The perfect καταπέπωκε leaves the shell where it now is — inside him.

sentences.t: Βαρούμενος δὲ τὰ σπλάγχνα καὶ ὀδυνώμενος ἔλεγε· « Δίκαια ἔγωγε πέπονθα, εἴγε πάντα περιφερῆ ᾠὰ πεπίστευκα. »
sentences.tr: Baroumenos de ta splanchna kai odynōmenos elege· « Dikaia egōge pepontha, eige panta peripherē ōia pepisteuka. »
sentences.l: And being weighed down in his innards and being in pain he was saying: « Justly indeed have I suffered, if I have in fact believed all round things to be eggs. »
sentences.i: Weighed down in his innards and in pain, he said: « I have got exactly what I deserved, if I really believed everything round was an egg. »
sentences.n: τὰ σπλάγχνα is an accusative of respect with the passive βαρούμενος: heavy in the part affected. δίκαια πέπονθα is the ordinary Greek for getting what one has coming. εἴγε, 'if indeed', concedes the folly rather than doubting it, and πεπίστευκα takes a double accusative — believed all round things eggs. Both perfects put the mistake behind him and its consequence still in him.

sentences.t: Διδάσκει ἡμᾶς ὁ λόγος ὅτι οἱ ἀδικάστως πρᾶγμα προσιόντες λανθάνουσιν ἑαυτοὺς περιπείροντες ἀτόποις.
sentences.tr: Didaskei hēmas ho logos hoti hoi adikastōs pragma prosiontes lanthanousin heautous peripeirontes atopois.
sentences.l: The story teaches us that those who approach a matter without judgment escape their own notice impaling themselves upon absurdities.
sentences.i: The story teaches us that those who go at a matter without judgment impale themselves on absurdities before they know it.
sentences.n: λανθάνω with a supplementary participle inverts the English: the finite verb carries the not-noticing and the participle carries the deed — 'they escape their own notice impaling themselves' is 'they impale themselves without noticing'. This turn is worth watching for; it recurs. ἀδικάστως is 'without a judgment passed', undiscriminating. περιπείρω is to run a thing through and fix it fast, which is what the shell has done. ἄτοπος is what is out of place, and so absurd.
